# Synthesis {.unnumbered .ch-page-heading}
:::

## Introduction
The chapters preceding this synthesis established the ecological and practical basis for using stone piles as a kōura habitat enhancement tool in the Rotorua Te Arawa lakes. Behavioural laboratory experiments (Chapter 2) tested kōura refuge use when exposed to novel catfish predators compared to native eel predators. This demonstrated that kōura spend more time in refuges when they are exposed to catfish than to eels. Kōura habitat use of lake shorelines was assessed with field observations (Chapter 3) executed at 60 locations across five lakes. This identified that habitats comprising complex rocky substrates and riparian vegetation support higher kōura abundance than muddy or emergent macrophyte habitats. In mesocosm trials (Chapter 4) four consecutive experiments were carried out to establish the preferred material and structure of artificially introduced habitats. The results showed that structure stability and complexity matter more than material type when kōura select shelter. The field deployment study (Chapter 5) deployed five stone piles along the shoreline of Lake Rotoiti and monitored kōura response over 18 months in a BACI design. Kōura colonised the structures rapidly, with occupancy and abundance consistently trending positive at stone pile sites relative to controls, though this effect did not reach statistical significance. Catfish showed no evidence of being attracted to the stone piles. This chapter (Chapter 6) synthesises the findings across all four chapters and discusses their wider interpretation. Two additional field trials, detailed in the appendices, were incorporated to extend the findings of Chapter 3-5 into conditions not covered by the previous chapters. These included a reintroduction attempt in Lake Ōkaro that tested the water quality boundary of habitat enhancement (see Appendix: Chapter 6 — Supplementary information), and a depth-gradient deployment in Lake Rotoiti that explored use of stone pile structures beyond wading depth (see Appendix: Chapter 6 — Supplementary information).

## Three stressors working together
Kōura decline in the Rotorua Te Arawa Lakes is driven by multiple compounding stressors, most prominently catfish predation, thermal stratification, and invasive macrophytes, which together operate at both the local sub-lake scale and the broader lake scale.

The behavioural response demonstrated in Chapter 2 showed that kōura had greater refuge use in response to the novel catfish predator than to the native eel. This finding is consistent with prey exhibiting heightened caution toward unfamiliar predators with which they share no evolutionary history [@Sih2023], and demonstrates that fear-induced behavioural suppression operates even in the absence of direct predation. An animal spending more time in refuge is an animal spending less time foraging, leading to slower growth and reduced reproductive output. This is the core mechanism behind the landscape of fear [@Laundre2001], where predators do not need to eat every prey individual to suppress a population, but their presence alone is sufficient to reshape how prey use habitats over space and time, and those behavioural changes carry demographic consequences. In the context of the Rotorua Te Arawa Lakes, this means that catfish potentially suppress kōura populations through two mechanisms simultaneously. Direct predation removes individuals and fear-induced behavioural change reduces the reproductive capacity of those that survive. Even if predation rates are reduced, population recovery under these conditions is likely to be slow, because the behaviour suppression can persist as long as catfish are present.

The lake-scale and sub-lake-scale patterns identified in Chapter 3 provide further evidence that kōura decline results from multiple interacting pressures rather than catfish predation alone. Oligotrophic lakes with no catfish had the highest overall kōura catches, while eutrophic lakes with catfish and anoxic stratification yielded substantially lower kōura numbers. At the sub-lake scale, structurally complex rocky shorelines were associated with higher kōura abundance, while excessive macrophyte cover was associated with lower densities, which is consistent with preferred kōura habitat in streams [@Usio2000; @Parkyn2004; @Jowett2008; @Parkyn2009]. These findings show that kōura abundance is shaped by stressors operating at both lake scale and sub-lake scale.

Habitat enhancement represents an important intervention under current pressures. The mesocosm trials (Chapter 4) showed that kōura preferentially select stable, crevice-rich structures, similar to the habitat characteristics that stone piles provide in the lake, suggesting that the positive trend in Chapter 5 reflects genuine preference rather than incidental use. Chapter 5 showed that stone piles in Lake Rotoiti attracted kōura densities approaching those on natural rocky substrates, despite the ongoing presence of catfish. While high-quality refuge does not eliminate the fear response, it provides kōura with locations where they can shelter effectively and emerge to forage in relative safety, remaining active and accessible to resources despite the continued presence of catfish [@Shave1994; @Adams2007; @Francis2019; @Zhao2024]. In catfish-invaded lakes where predator eradication is not feasible, habitat provision may therefore help a remnant kōura population persist and gradually recover rather than decline towards local extinction.

Kōura use of stone pile refuges in the littoral zone was strongly seasonal (Chapter 5), with greatest use during summer and autumn when stratification and catfish shoreline use simultaneously peak. During these periods, deep-water oxygen depletion restricts access to deeper habitats, while increased catfish activity in the littoral zone may expose kōura to greater predation risk, effectively compressing them into a narrower band of suitable habitat. In winter, when stratification breaks down and deeper waters are reoxygenated, kōura may redistribute into deeper habitats or simply remain within existing shallow refuges once predation and thermal pressure ease [@Devcich1979]. Climate projections suggest that this seasonal habitat constraint will intensify as surface waters warm, stratification becomes stronger and more persistent, and deep-water hypoxia and anoxia become more frequent and prolonged [@Jane2021; @Woolway2021; @Lee2025]. Chapter 1 documents a decline in suitable habitat for kōura over the last 20 years across eleven lakes, calculated as the proportion of the lakebed area meeting dissolved oxygen and temperature thresholds for kōura. For example, Lake Ōkāreka showed a statistically significant annual decline of 0.4% in liveable habitat per year, indicating that the suitable habitat window is narrowing under current conditions, not just future ones (see Appendix: Chapter 1 — Supplementary information).

## Kōura monitoring approaches
A key insight from this research is that standard passive netting, while effective for estimating relative kōura abundance across sites, cannot distinguish whether kōura are actively using a specific structure or are simply present in the surrounding area. This distinction matters directly for interpreting the Chapter 5 results: higher catches near stone piles were taken as evidence of greater habitat use, but passive netting alone cannot confirm structural preference. @Johnsen2008 monitored their stone addition site using both diving surveys and baited traps over 13 years, finding a large increase in noble crayfish abundance using both methods. More structurally complex habitat may also introduce a systematic detection bias in the opposite direction: kōura sheltering within stone piles may become genuinely harder to catch or observe if they can forage on snails and other invertebrates within the structure itself, without needing to emerge at all [@Francis2019]. A similar pattern has been reported in North American lakes containing largemouth bass (*Micropterus salmoides*) (W. Perry, pers. comm.). This limitation influenced the monitoring approaches across the thesis, from netting in Chapter 3 and 5 toward direct observation methods in later trials (see Appendix: Chapter 6 — Supplementary information), where spotlighting, Remotely Operated Vehicle (ROV) surveys, and diving allowed kōura to be observed on structures directly.

Traditional Māori harvesting methods using tau kōura with whakaweku (bundles of bracken fern *Pteridium esculentum*) have proven effective for kōura monitoring in lakes and stream habitats [@Kusabs2009; @Kusabs2018] but presented two specifics constraints in this research context. In the shallow wave-exposed zone of the study lakes, wave action destabilises the whakaweku, reducing their effectiveness as a consistent shelter substrate. A further limitation in the context of this thesis is that whakaweku creates habitat. Using it to assess whether stone piles attract kōura would confound the monitoring tool with the intervention, making it difficult to determine whether kōura are responding to the stone pile or the whakaweku itself.

Passive netting with single-winged fyke nets and bait traps were therefore used throughout the monitoring described in Chapters 3 and 5. Traps were baited with trout flesh in Chapter 3 and catfish flesh in Chapter 5. When comparing catches at Lake Rotoiti sites, no difference was found between bait types. This was expected as kōura scavenge carcasses of dead fish without bias towards native or non-native species [@MacNeil2025]. Trout as bait yielded a mean CPUE of 0.63 kōura per trap per night (95% CI: 0–1.42; *n* = 12 trap nights) and catfish bait 0.65 kōura per trap per night (95% CI: 0.43–0.90; *n* = 135). Unbaited fyke nets had a notably higher CPUE of 2.55 kōura per trap per night (95% CI: 1.89–3.31; *n* = 148), consistent with their larger net opening and longer fishing lead. However, 24-hour passive netting provides an approximation of local abundance rather than direct evidence of habitat use. As noted above, trap catches cannot distinguish presence from increased use of habitat structure. For Chapter 5, higher catches near stone piles were therefore interpreted as indicating greater use of the structures as habitat. In structurally complex habitats, fyke nets must be placed flat on the sediment to fish effectively; on rocky substrates this is often not possible, and kōura may pass beneath the net opening entirely. At the deep structures built in Lake Rotoiti, more active monitoring approaches were applied including spotlighting from the jetty, ROV surveys and human dive surveys (see Appendix: Chapter 6 — Supplementary information). These methods allow direct observation of kōura using the structures and are easier to execute over depth than netting. However, these direct methods capture only the moment of observation, and the detection bias introduced by structural complexity means that even direct observations may underestimate true habitat use if kōura remain sheltered during surveys. Passive Integrated Transponder (PIT) tagging, combined with an antenna array installed beneath or around a structure, would allow individual kōura to be tracked continuously without requiring their emergence or capture, resolving the detection bias identified above. The same approach could also support mark-recapture estimates of population size at stone pile sites, complementing its use for tracking movement and habitat use. PIT tagging is relatively low-cost and widely used in fish and crayfish movement studies and represents a promising direction for confirming genuine structural preference in future stone pile deployment [@Bubb2006; @Westhoff2013].

Additional monitoring techniques including environmental DNA (eDNA), remote underwater video (RUV), baited remote underwater video (BRUV), and passive acoustic monitoring, would be valuable to develop and trial. Comparative studies suggest that trapping, RUV, BRUV perform similarly for crayfish detection while eDNA has failed to detect crayfish in similar stream systems [@Harwood2025; @Harwood2026]. Conversely, eDNA has detected invasive crayfish in lakes where trapping alone could not [@Dougherty2016], suggesting it may be better suited to lake-scale presence-absence assessments than to evaluate kōura use of specific structures. Passive acoustics offer a complementary approach as crayfish produce distinctive sounds during movement and feeding, and acoustic methods have shown potential for identifying crayfish behaviour in field and laboratory settings [@Buscaino2012; @DeVita2023]. Application in marine systems has advanced further, including detection of spiny lobsters over great distances [@Jezequel2020; @Jezequel2023]; whether passive acoustic monitoring is sensitive enough to detect kōura activity in the complex acoustic environment of a lake littoral zone remains untested.

## What habitat enhancement can and cannot fix
In Chapter 3, shoreline habitat surveys across five Te Arawa Lakes showed that kōura were most consistently associated with complex rocky habitats and riparian vegetation [@Jowett2008; @Kusabs2015b]. Locations where this substrate has been lost or never existed are therefore logical candidates for stone pile deployment. Chapter 4 confirmed that structural permanence and complexity are the decisive factors in kōura shelter selection, and stone piles deliver both [@Streissl2002]. In lakes where populations are declining, stone piles can help a remnant population persist and create habitat stepping stones that lower the cost of dispersal between patches, keeping populations more connected while broader lake conditions improve. Stone piles may also physically suppress invasive macrophytes at the placement site, as demonstrated by the stone pile at 4 m depth in the deep Rotoiti case study, though whether this reflects sustained suppression or slow regrowth of macrophytes remains untested. Chapter 5 demonstrates that stone piles represent a specific type of intervention that operates differently from stressor removal.

Unlike water quality improvement or catfish management, structural habitat addition does not require these broader stressors to be fully controlled first, although the magnitude and persistence of those benefits will depend on local conditions, particularly trophic state, the severity and duration of bottom water anoxia during summer stratification, and catfish density. Stone piles function as a buffer against stressors that cannot be eliminated at lake scale. Catfish eradication would likely require broad-spectrum piscicides or complete lake drawdown which would also kill or displace native fish species [@Dedual2019]. Future biotechnologies, including gene drives and pathogens that target only the invasive species, could eventually provide additional options, but these tools are still in early, experimental stages of development [@Thresher2014; @Kopf2019; @Teem2020], making current eradication impractical at the Rotoiti and Rotorua scale. The expected future increase in lake water temperature will intensify thermal stratification under continued climate warming, which will benefit catfish more than kōura [@Woolway2021; @Lee2025]. When these stressors cannot be removed habitat enhancement becomes a practical management tool whose importance grows even as worsening conditions constrain how much benefit it can ultimately deliver.

Whether habitat enhancement delivers population-level benefits depends on whether habitat availability is genuinely limiting. In a Norwegian lake where muddy substrates limited noble crayfish (*Astacus astacus*) distribution, adding rocky substrate to previously unproductive areas resulted in colonisation and improved harvest [@Johnsen2008]. In that system, habitat was the constraint, and removing it produced a clear response. Similarly, structure additions to streams have been shown to improve success of crayfish restocking efforts [@Huolila1997]. In both cases, suitable habitat was the limiting factor that limited the crayfish population. The situation in the Rotorua Te Arawa Lakes is more complex as habitat availability is not independently limiting but becomes limiting in combination with other stressors. Thermal stratification and invasive macrophytes compress kōura into a narrow littoral zone, and catfish predation within that zone forces kōura into refuges, which are scarce in the predominant sandy littoral zone of Lake Rotoiti. The lack of suitable habitat is therefore one compounding stressor among several: structure cannot compensate for water that is unbreathable, nor can it fully counteract sustained predation pressure.

Kōura recovery is bounded by a ceiling set by whichever stressor is currently most limiting. This is consistent with the Liebig–Sprengel "law of the minimum": population recovery is limited by the scarcest resource or most severe stressor, not by the average condition of the system [@Holmes2018]. Where water quality is poor or catfish predation is intense, that ceiling is low, as demonstrated by the anoxic event in Lake Ōkaro (see Appendix: Chapter 6 — Supplementary information). Where conditions are already favourable the ceiling is correspondingly higher, consistent with  findings in Chapter 3 that lakes with the best water quality, most complex habitat, and no catfish support the highest kōura abundance. As catfish likely cannot be eradicated at lake scale, and thermal stratification will intensify under continued climate warming, the ceiling is unlikely to rise on its own in lakes like Rotoiti and Rotorua. This does not make habitat enhancement less valuable; it means structural refuge becomes more necessary even though its maximum benefit stays limited. Habitat enhancement should therefore be used alongside water quality and predator management, not instead of them.

## Future direction

### Scaling habitat enhancement 
The five stone pile sites monitored in Chapter 5 represent a proof-of-concept deployment rather than a management-scale intervention. The positive but non-significant trend in kōura abundance suggest that the 18-month monitoring period was insufficient to detect population-level responses. Continued monitoring of the existing Rotoiti stone piles would determine whether the positive trends continue and reveal longer-term population-level effects.

Beyond continued monitoring, scaling deployment to additional sites, depths, and lakes would test whether the Rotoiti results are generalised across the Te Arawa lakes. Lake Rotorua, which also has declining kōura populations and limited natural rocky habitats, would be a logical next deployment location. The deep stone pile case study in this chapter demonstrated that deployment across a depth gradient extends the range of conditions under which kōura can use the structures and further deployment should incorporate this principle. Standardised monitoring protocols across sites, including spotlighting, fyke netting, and ROV surveys, would allow for a cross-lake comparison of the habitat enhancement as a management tool.

### Community involvement in kōura restoration
One of the practical strengths of stone pile deployment is that construction does not require specialist equipment or expertise. Both the Rotoiti and Ōkaro deployments in this thesis were built by hand using locally sourced materials, demonstrating that this kind of restoration work is accessible to a wide range of participants.

Residents living along the lakes could contribute directly, for example by replacing unproductive hard structures, like retaining walls that provide no habitat value, with stones and rocks or by placing stones under jetties where they are out of the way of boating and swimming yet provide effective shelter for kōura. Some residents around the Rotorua Te Arawa Lakes have already independently built kōura habitat structures using similar principles (@fig-koura-structures-diy), demonstrating both the appeal and feasibility of community-led habitat enhancement. Future community contributions would benefit from using natural materials that will not degrade over time, and from maximising crevice diversity, as the more hiding places the structures create, the wider the range of kōura life stages it can support. Stones in the 100–300 mm range, as used in this study, provide abundant shelter space when stacked together, are simple to deploy and persist in the lake without introducing pollutants.

![Home-made kōura habitats by local residents. Left: Kōura pipes by Mark Thomson at Lake Rotoiti. Right: Kōura wheels by Mark Robinson at Lake Tarawera.](images/Koura_structures_diy.png){#fig-koura-structures-diy width=65%}

### Kōura restoration in a Te Arawa context
Kōura are taonga, a treasured species with deep cultural significance for Te Arawa iwi. The decline of kōura observed in the lakes [@Kusabs2026] is not only an ecological loss but a cultural one. Increasing shelter availability may attract kōura and support population recovery, with potential benefits for cultural practices. Localised kōura harvesting currently occurs at Cherry Bay (Ōkahuroroa Bay) in Lake Rotoiti where regular monitoring using the tau kōura (and whakaweku) in conjunction with regular aquatic weed spraying and catfish netting has potentially already created a degree of structural complexity in the bay. This suggests a model for cultural kōura restoration in Lake Rotoiti: identifying areas with favourable lake bathymetry, maintaining regular spraying of aquatic weeds and active catfish removal, and creating habitat using whakaweku, tau kōura, and potentially stone piles to establish dedicated kōura reserves within in the lake that could support renewed cultural harvest activity. This is a suggestion for future research and management to consider together with Te Arawa.

The evidence in this thesis has direct implications for the restoration of cultural kōura harvest in Lake Rotoiti. Given the compounding effects of multiple stressors, and the expectation that climate change and invasive species pressure will both persist, kōura are likely to remain present in these lakes, but lake-wide populations are unlikely to reach the abundance historically required for cultural harvest while catfish predation remains. Catfish and kōura are likely already setting into a new predator-prey equilibrium in lakes where sustained, catfish control is not feasible. In this context, management priorities may be better directed toward protecting kōura populations that remain strong in lakes without catfish, like Rotomā, Ōkataina, Ōkāreka, and Tarawera, by preventing the spread of catfish and invasive macrophytes into these systems, rather than solely focusing on recovery in already catfish-invaded lakes.

Rather than a single outcome, kōura recovery toward cultural harvest abundance can be understood as a staged process. The first step is to prevent localised extinction. Findings from this thesis suggest that rocky habitat or stone piles are a useful tool for sustaining remnant kōura populations as the lake warms and habitat compression intensifies. Stabilising the decline is a necessary foundation before broader recovery becomes possible. The second step is reducing nutrient loading to reverse lake eutrophication and unlock deep-water habitat during summer stratification. Lake Taupō illustrates what is possible when water quality is not limiting, as sixty years of catchment-scale management have kept the lake oligotrophic with deep waters remaining oxygenated through summer, giving kōura a place to coexist in the presence of catfish [@West2026]. To achieve this in already eutrophic lakes such as Rotorua and Rotoiti would require active reversal of existing nutrient loading.

## Conclusion
Kōura populations in some Rotorua Te Arawa Lakes have declined by 76-91% since 2003. Freshwater species decline is rarely driven by a single stressor, and kōura in these lakes face several acting simultaneously: predation and fear-induced behavioural suppression caused by catfish; thermal stratification, which compresses suitable habitat into the shallow littoral zone, precisely where catfish predation pressure is greatest; and invasive macrophytes, which further constrict the habitat available to kōura. This thesis investigated whether, within this compounding-stressor context, habitat enhancement could provide a practical means of supporting kōura recovery.

The findings of this thesis are best understood through the concept of a stressor “ceiling” on recovery: kōura population recovery is bounded not by the average condition of a lake but by whichever stressor is currently most limiting. Eutrophication acts as something of a master stressor in this system: reducing nitrogen and phosphorus loading would also ease the macrophyte and hypoxia pressures. Habitat enhancement cannot fix eutrophication; that requires action at the catchment scale, which is fundamentally a political and economic choice rather than an ecological one.

Habitat enhancement alone is unlikely to restore lake-wide kōura populations to the abundance needed for cultural harvest while eutrophication and catfish predation persist. What this thesis shows is that structural habitat enhancement can be used as a tool to reduce the risk of localised extinction, by providing refuge to mediate the predation pressure. Bringing kōura populations back to the abundance needed for cultural harvest will require action on those wider stressors too, particularly nutrient loading and invasive macrophyte spread. Until then, habitat enhancement remains a practical step that lake managers can take now.
